title: Effects of Acute Aerobic Exercise on Sequentially Administered Cognitive Tasks Reflecting Working Memory Subcomponents and Heart Rate Variability.
abstract: Although acute aerobic exercise selectively influences specific subcomponents of working memory, whether such benefits transfer to a subsequent cognitive task engaging a different domain remains unclear. Forty-seven participants completed, in randomized order, an exercise condition (10 min of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise) and a control condition, each immediately followed by a visuospatial construction task (the Equilibrio game) and a 2-Back working memory task, with heart rate variability (HRV) recorded throughout. Completion time on the Equilibrio task was significantly shorter following exercise than following control,= 292.5,= -2.873,= .004,= -0.481. In contrast, no significant between-condition differences emerged on any behavioral parameter of the 2-Back task, including completion time, accuracy, hit rate, discrimination sensitivity ('), and response bias (; alls > 0.05). During the 2-Back task, however, sympathetic indices (SNS Index, Stress Index, LF/HF ratio) were significantly elevated and parasympathetic/vagal indices (RMSSD, SDNN, PNS Index, HF n.u.) were significantly suppressed following exercise, despite unchanged behavior. These findings indicate that exercise-induced cognitive benefit is task-specific and does not extend to a subsequent task engaging a different working memory subcomponent, even as autonomic activation persists. This dissociation challenges general-arousal accounts of exercise-cognition effects and supports a domain-specific, timing-sensitive framework.
